newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch resigned as EU vets extend pig export ban.
newsitem.headline: Dutch resigned as EU vets extend pig export ban.

text.p: The Netherlands on Wednesday greeted a European Union decision to extend an export ban on Dutch pigs because of swine fever as "understandable" in view of recent further outbreaks.

EU veterinary experts earlier voted to maintain the ban for a further week after fresh outbreaks of swine fever in the south of the country, believed originally to have been caused by animals imported from Germany.

"In the light of the spread of swine fever in (southern) Brabant (province) over the last week, I think it understandable that Brussels wishes to monitor the situation for another week," Dutch farm minister Jozias van Aartsen said.
An interim extension of another week had been considered inevitable, Van Aartsen said, adding he welcomed the EU standing veterinary committee's decision not to tighten controls further.
"It seems we are handling (the situation) very well," he said.
The Dutch farmers' organisation LTO said it hoped that the ban, which has dealt a major blow to the $2.7 billion Dutch pig export industry, would not remain in place for more than a fortnight.
It told the Dutch news agency ANP no new outbreaks had been signalled for several days and research into various stages of the disease indicated that the epidemic might have peaked.
EU veterinary experts met in Brussels today to review measures the Dutch have taken to contain and eradicate the highly contagious disease, which is not harmful to humans.
EU farm inspectors who conducted a three-day inspection in Brabant where the disease broke out reported to the committee that the country's swine fever controls were excellent, Dutch diplomats said.
"That was the report used although there was criticism that insufficient blood samples had been taken at the start of the epidemic," a Dutch diplomat in Brussels said.
Dutch officials also reported on the latest measures taken to halt the spread of the virus.
In the most dramatic development to date, the government said on Monday it would buy and destroy 800,000 pigs which cannot be marketed because of a ban on transporting livestock.
The European Union will meet some 70 percent of the cost, estimated at 150 million guilders ($80 million).

Since the first case was confirmed on February 4, swine fever has been detected on 18 farms in Brabant. All but one fall within an area of the province containing roughly one fifth of the country's 14 million pigs.
Some 35,000 pigs from infected or neighbouring farms have already been destroyed and transport of any kind of livestock has been banned in a 10 km (six mile) radius of those farms.
Pig markets have been closed in the whole of the country to prevent the infection spreading.
Last week the EU slapped a ban on the export of live pigs from the Netherlands, except the four northernmost provinces.
The U.S. had already halted imports of Dutch pork products and Poland had closed its borders to Dutch pigs and pork.
In 1996 the Netherlands exported almost a million tonnes of pigs and pork products, about 60 percent of its production, bringing in around 5.1 billion guilders ($2.7 billion).
Germany is the main foreign market for Dutch pigs and pork products taking 38 percent of all Dutch exports, followed by Italy (22 percent), Britain (11 percent) and France (eight percent).
